theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: In cash handling, what is a "float"?
options: The total of all the sales taken during one shift
A set amount of cash put in the drawer to give change
The money a cashier keeps as a tip at the end of the day
A list of the prices for all items sold at the bar

questions.stem: At the start of your shift, the supervisor gives you a float. What should you do first?
options: Put it straight in the drawer without opening the bag
Use it to buy small items the bar needs for the day
Count it with the supervisor and sign that it is correct
Leave it in the safe until you run out of change

questions.stem: Why should a float hold plenty of small notes and coins?
options: So the drawer looks full to the guests
So you can give change to the first guests
So the float is lighter to carry to the bank
So the shift report will balance by itself

questions.stem: Which of these should you check before you open the cash point for service?
options: That the guest list for the night is printed
That the till roll, pens and card terminal work
That the safe code has been written on the till
That the menu prices are covered with tape

questions.stem: Which of these is a non-cash payment?
options: A debit card
A J$1,000 note
A US$20 note
A J$20 coin

questions.stem: A guest staying at a villa asks to put her bar bill on her room. What is this called?
options: A cash advance to the room
A refund to the room
A paid-out from the room
A charge to the room account

questions.stem: A guest's bill is J$3,450. She pays with a J$5,000 note. How much change do you give?
Why do you leave the guest's note on top of the drawer, not inside it, until you have given the change?
options: So that the note can dry out if it was wet in a pocket
So there is no argument about which note was given
So the guest can easily take it back if they change their mind
So the supervisor can see it from the office

questions.stem: What is the best way to give change to a guest?
options: Put all the notes and coins in one pile on the counter
Hand it over quickly without saying the amount
Count it back aloud, from the bill up to the amount paid
Drop it into the tip jar and let the guest take what is theirs

questions.stem: When you check a J$ note to see if it is real, which method is good practice?
options: Ask the guest to sign the back of the note for you
Check only that the colour looks about right to you
Fold it in half to see if it tears along the crease
Feel it, look at it and tilt it to see its features

questions.stem: You think a note a guest has given you may be counterfeit (fake). What should you do?
options: Hand it back and tell everyone nearby that it is fake
Accept it quietly and hide it under the tray of the drawer
Tear it in half so that nobody can try to use it again
Stay polite and call your supervisor, as the rules say

questions.stem: Who sets the exchange rate you use when a guest pays a J$ bill in US$?
options: The guest, using a rate from a phone app
You, using the rate from last week's paper
The tour rep who brought the guest to the property
The property, from the rate given for the day

questions.stem: For this question only, use a practice rate of J$150 = US$1. A guest pays a J$4,500 bill in US dollars. How much is that in US$?
options: US$25
US$45
US$30
US$35

questions.stem: For this question only, use a practice rate of J$150 = US$1. A guest gives US$20 for a J$2,400 bill, and change is given in J$. How much change do you give?
A guest pays a J$ bill with US$ cash. What should the receipt show?
options: The amount in US$, the rate used and the J$ total
Only the guest's room number, written large at the top
The cashier's own name, phone number and home address
The amount of the tip the guest is expected to leave

questions.stem: A guest pays with a card that has a chip. What is the usual way to take the payment?
options: Swipe the card and keep it until the guest leaves
Write the card number on the bill and type it in later
Ask the guest to tell you the PIN so you can enter it
Let the guest insert or tap it and key in the PIN

questions.stem: Why must you never ask a guest to tell you their PIN?
options: Because the PIN is only needed for cash payments
Because only the cardholder should know and key in the PIN
Because the terminal will print the PIN on the guest's receipt
Because the bank sends the PIN to the cashier by text

questions.stem: The terminal shows "Declined" for a guest's card. What should you do?
options: Tell the guest loudly that the card has been refused
Tell the guest quietly and ask for another way to pay
Keep trying the card until the terminal accepts it
Cut the card in half and give the pieces back to the guest

questions.stem: Before taking a card payment, what may the property ask you to check on the card?
options: The guest's home address on the back
How much money is left on the card
The bank's phone number on the front
The expiry date and the name

questions.stem: Before you charge a meal to a guest's room, what must you check?
options: That the guest has a car parked in the property's lot
That the guest has eaten at the bar before
That the name and room number match the records
That the guest has paid a tip in cash first

questions.stem: Why do you ask the guest to sign the bill when it is charged to the room?
options: So the guest can take the signature home as a souvenir
So the kitchen knows who ordered the food
So there is proof the guest agreed to the charge
So the bill does not need to show any prices

questions.stem: A guest gives you a voucher for a free dinner from a tour company. What should you do first?
options: Throw it in the bin as soon as the guest has finished eating
Charge the guest anyway and keep the voucher too
Give the guest cash for the value of the voucher
Check that it is valid and meant for this property

questions.stem: A guest pays with a phone payment app that the property accepts. What must you see before the guest leaves?
options: The guest's phone password written on the bill
A confirmation that the payment went through
A photo of the guest's bank card
The guest's bank account balance

questions.stem: Why must every payment get a receipt?
options: It is proof of payment for both sides
It lets the guest skip paying GCT on the bill
It is needed only if the guest asks for a refund
It tells the guest how much to tip the staff

questions.stem: A guest asks what GCT on the bill is. What is the correct explanation?
options: It is a tip that the staff add for themselves
It is a charge for using a card to pay
It is the tax on sales, charged at the current rate
It is a fee only foreign guests have to pay

questions.stem: A bill shows a service charge. Where do you find out what rate is used?
options: From the guest, who chooses the amount
From the property's policy or the supervisor
From the menu of another hotel down the road
From the bank that supplies the card terminal

questions.stem: You keyed in the wrong item and the guest has not paid yet. What is cancelling it on the POS usually called?
options: A refund
A discount
A void
A paid-out

questions.stem: Who must usually approve a refund before you give it?
options: A supervisor or manager
Any guest in the queue
The cashier on the next shift
The guest's travel agent

questions.stem: Where is the safest place to count a large amount of cash?
options: At the bar counter, where guests can see you
At the pool, where the light is good
In the staff canteen at lunch time
In a secure office, out of public view

questions.stem: Your drawer is holding a lot of large notes in the middle of a busy shift. What should you do?
options: Take them home for safe keeping overnight
Put them in your pocket until the shift ends
Move them to the safe with a signed record
Give them to a regular guest to hold

questions.stem: You must leave the cash point for a moment. What should you do?
options: Leave the drawer open so others can serve
Ask a guest to watch the drawer for you
Leave the key in the drawer lock for speed
Lock the drawer and take the key with you

questions.stem: A person threatens you and demands the cash. What is the safest thing to do?
options: Stay calm, do as they say and do not fight back
Refuse and try to hold on to the cash drawer
Chase the person out of the building
Shout at them so they get frightened off

questions.stem: When you cash up, which amount do you take away from the total cash counted to find the cash takings?
options: The float
The GCT total
The card total
The room charges

questions.stem: After cashing up, the cash counted is J$500 less than the POS report. What should you do?
options: Put in J$500 of your own money and say nothing
Record the shortage and report it to the supervisor
Change the figures on the report so that they match
Take J$500 from the float for the next shift

questions.stem: Why should a cashier never "fix" a cash over or short by moving money between shifts?
options: Because the bank charges a fee for each change
Because it makes the drawer too heavy
Because it hides errors and possible theft
Because guests may see the money moved

questions.stem: When you cash up, why do you count the card slips or card report as well as the cash?
options: So the guest can be called and thanked
So the full card numbers can be written down in a book
So the cashier knows how much to tip
So all payment types match the POS total

questions.stem: How should the cash takings be sent to the bank or the office safe?
options: In an open envelope carried by a guest
In the cashier's own handbag after work
In a sealed, signed bag with a deposit slip
Loose in the drawer, left at the bar overnight

questions.stem: Why must cash-up sheets be filled in neatly and signed?
options: They are a record that can be checked later
They are given to guests with their bills
They are used to work out the staff rota
They are pinned on the board for all to see

questions.stem: Why does a card receipt usually show only the last four digits of the card number?
options: To save paper and ink on the till roll
Because the rest is a code only staff use
Because four digits are all the bank needs
To protect the cardholder from card fraud

questions.stem: A guest says their bill is wrong. What should you do first?
options: Listen, then check the bill with them
Tell them the POS is never wrong
Ask them to pay first and complain later
Call security to stand beside the guest

questions.stem: A guest is unsure what the total on the bill includes. How should you help?
options: Go through each item and charge with them
Tell them to read the bill again on their own
Say that all bills include a large tip
Take the bill away and print it again later

questions.stem: A friend comes to your bar and asks you not to ring up their drinks. What should you do?
options: Agree, as long as it is just a few drinks
Ring up only half of the drinks they order
Let them pay you cash straight into your pocket
Politely refuse and ring up every sale

questions.stem: Why do you keep notes in the drawer face up and sorted by value?
options: So the drawer looks nice to guests
So the money stays cool in hot weather
So you can give change fast and count it right
So the notes do not need to be counted at the end

questions.stem: A guest at the bar asks you to change US$200 into J$ cash. The bar does not offer exchange. What should you do?
options: Direct them to the front desk or another licensed place
Change it with your own money at your own rate
Ask another guest to swap the money with them
Take the money and bring back J$ the next day

questions.stem: Why must each cashier log in to the POS with their own user name?
options: So the screen shows their favourite colours
So each sale can be traced to the right person
So the POS can print in a bigger font
So the cashier can see other staff's sales

What do the letters GCT stand for on a Jamaican bill?

essays.stem: Describe how you would get a cash point ready before you open for service.
essays.modelAnswer: I wash my hands, check my uniform and name badge and arrive on time. I collect my float from the supervisor and count it with them, note by note and coin by coin, then we both sign the float sheet to show it is correct. I place the notes face up in the drawer, sorted by value, with the coins in their own sections. I log in to the POS with my own user name and check that the date, prices and printer work. I make sure there are spare till rolls, pens, bill folders and receipt books. I switch on the card terminal and check it is connected and has paper. I check the day's exchange rate and any specials or vouchers I need to know about. Finally, I make sure the drawer is closed and locked until the first guest comes.
markingPoints: Collects the float and counts it with the supervisor
Signs the float sheet to show the amount is correct
Sets out notes and coins sorted and face up in the drawer
Logs in with own user name and checks the POS and card terminal work
Has supplies ready (till rolls, pens, folders) and knows the day's rate and specials

essays.stem: Describe, step by step, how you take a cash payment from a guest and give the right change.
essays.modelAnswer: I present the bill and tell the guest the total clearly. When the guest hands me the money, I say the amount out loud, for example, "Out of five thousand dollars." I check the note is genuine by feeling it, looking at it and tilting it. I place the note on top of the drawer, not inside it, while I key the amount into the POS. The POS shows the change due. I take the change from the drawer and count it back to the guest, starting from the bill total and counting up to the amount they gave me. Only then do I put the guest's note into the drawer and close it. I give the guest the receipt and thank them by name. If the guest says the change is wrong, the note still on top of the drawer helps to settle it.
markingPoints: States the total and says the amount received out loud
Checks the note is genuine
Keeps the note on top of the drawer until the change is given
Counts the change back from the bill up to the amount paid
Closes the drawer, gives a receipt and thanks the guest

essays.stem: Explain how you check bank notes to see if they are real, and what you do if you think a note is counterfeit.
essays.modelAnswer: I check every large note as I take it. I feel the note: real notes have a firm feel and some raised printing. I look at it against the light for the watermark and the security thread, and I tilt it to see features that change colour or shine. If the property has an ultraviolet lamp, I use it as I was trained. I compare it with a note I know is real. If I think a note is counterfeit, I stay calm and polite and do not accuse the guest, because they may not know. I keep the note, do not hand it back to be used elsewhere, and call my supervisor at once. The supervisor follows the property's procedure, which may mean telling the police. I write down what happened, the time and a description of the person.
markingPoints: Feels the note for texture and raised print
Looks at the watermark and thread and tilts it to see the security features
Compares it with a genuine note or uses a UV lamp if the property has one
Stays calm and polite and does not accuse the guest
Calls the supervisor at once, follows procedure and records what happened

essays.stem: A guest wants to pay a J$ bill with US$ cash. Explain how you deal with this.
essays.modelAnswer: First I check that the property accepts US$ at my cash point. I use only the exchange rate the property has set for the day, never one the guest or I choose. I tell the guest the rate and work out the bill in US$ on the POS or a calculator, and I show the guest the working so they can see it is fair. I check the US$ notes for damage and to see that they are genuine. I give change in the currency the property's policy says, usually J$, and I count it back clearly. The receipt shows the J$ total, the US$ amount received, the rate used and the change given. At the cash-up I record the US$ separately from the J$, so both can be checked against the report.
markingPoints: Checks the property accepts US$ and uses only the property's rate for the day
Tells the guest the rate and shows the working
Checks the US$ notes are genuine and in good condition
Gives change as the policy says and counts it back
Receipt and cash-up record both currencies and the rate used

essays.stem: Describe how you take a card payment safely, and what you do if the card is declined.
essays.modelAnswer: I key the correct amount into the card terminal and check it with the guest. I hand the terminal to the guest, or take it to their table, so the card stays in their sight. The guest inserts or taps the card and keys in their own PIN, and I look away while they do it. I never ask for the PIN and never write down the card number. When the terminal shows the payment is approved, I give the guest their copy of the slip, keep the property's copy for the cash-up and return the card. If the card is declined, I tell the guest quietly and politely, so other guests do not hear. I may try once more if the property allows, then ask if they have another way to pay. If there is a problem, I call my supervisor.
markingPoints: Keys and checks the correct amount with the guest
Keeps the card in the guest's sight; the guest keys in their own PIN
Never asks for the PIN or writes down the card number
Waits for approval, gives the slip and returns the card
Handles a declined card quietly and politely, asks for another way to pay or calls the supervisor

essays.stem: Explain the checks you make before charging a restaurant or bar bill to a guest's room, and why each check matters.
essays.modelAnswer: I ask the guest for their name and room number, or for their key card, and I check these against the guest list on the POS so that the charge goes on the right account. I check that the room is allowed to take charges, because some guests pay cash only or have a credit limit. I may check a photo ID or the guest's wristband if the property asks for it. I ask the guest to check the bill and sign it, with their name and room number printed clearly, because the signature is proof that they agreed to the charge. I post the charge to the room straight away so it is on their folio before they check out. I never say the room number out loud, so other people cannot hear it.
markingPoints: Checks name and room number (or key card) against the records
Checks the account can take charges or has a credit limit
Checks ID or wristband where the property requires it
Gets the bill checked and signed as proof of agreement
Posts the charge promptly and keeps the room number private

essays.stem: Describe how you cash up and reconcile your drawer at the end of a shift.
essays.modelAnswer: I close the drawer to new sales and print the shift report from the POS, as the property's procedure says. In a quiet, secure place I count all the cash, note by note and coin by coin, and write the totals for each value on the cash-up sheet. I count the J$ and the US$ separately. I take away the float and put it aside for the next shift. What is left is the cash takings. I add up the card slips, room charge slips and vouchers. I compare each total with the POS report. If the figures match, I sign the sheet. If there is a shortage or an overage, I count again, then record it honestly and report it to the supervisor. I never cover a difference with my own money. The takings go in a sealed, signed bag for the safe.
markingPoints: Prints the shift report and counts the cash in a secure place
Counts J$ and US$ separately and records each value on the sheet
Removes the float to find the takings
Totals card slips, room charges and vouchers and compares all with the report
Recounts, records and reports any difference; seals and signs the takings bag

essays.stem: Explain how you keep cash safe during a shift at a bar or front desk.
essays.modelAnswer: I keep the drawer closed and locked between sales, and I never leave the cash point without locking it and taking the key, or logging off the POS. I only open the drawer when I am making a sale. I do not count large amounts in front of guests. When the drawer holds a lot of large notes, I make a safe drop as the property says, with a signed record and a witness. I do not let other staff use my drawer or my login. I keep my own money and bag away from the cash point. If someone threatens me, I stay calm, do what they say and do not fight, because my life is worth more than the money. Afterwards I raise the alarm, call the supervisor and the police, and write down what I saw.
markingPoints: Keeps the drawer closed and locked; locks or logs off when leaving
Does not count cash in public view
Makes recorded safe drops when the drawer holds too much
Does not share the drawer or login; keeps own money away
In a robbery stays calm, does not resist, then reports

essays.stem: Explain why voids and refunds must be approved and recorded, and describe how you deal with one.
essays.modelAnswer: A void cancels an item before the guest pays, and a refund gives money back after the guest has paid. Both take money out of the day's sales, so they could be used to hide theft. That is why the property wants a supervisor to approve them and a record of each one. If I make a mistake on a bill, or a guest returns something, I tell my supervisor straight away. The supervisor checks the reason and approves it on the POS with their own code. I write the reason, the amount, the time and both our names on the void or refund sheet, and keep any receipt. For a card refund, the money goes back to the same card. At the cash-up the voids and refunds are checked against the report.
markingPoints: Explains the difference between a void and a refund
Says why approval is needed (they reduce sales and could hide theft)
Gets a supervisor to check and approve
Records the reason, amount, time and names, and keeps the receipt
Refunds to the same payment method and checks them at cash-up

essays.stem: Compare cash and non-cash payments. Give one advantage and one risk of each for the property, and say how a cashier lowers the risks.
essays.modelAnswer: Cash is paid at once and costs the property no bank fees, which is an advantage. Its risks are theft, counterfeit notes and mistakes with change. The cashier lowers these by checking notes, counting change back, keeping the drawer locked, making safe drops and cashing up carefully. Non-cash payments, such as debit and credit cards, phone payments and room charges, are quick, and the property does not have to keep so much cash on site. Their risks are card fraud, declined cards, disputes and charges going to the wrong room. The cashier lowers these by letting the guest key in their own PIN, waiting for approval, checking the name and room number, getting the bill signed, and keeping card details private. Both kinds of payment need a receipt and a careful record.
markingPoints: An advantage of cash (paid at once, no bank fees)
A risk of cash (theft, fakes, wrong change) and how it is lowered
An advantage of non-cash (quick, less cash kept on site)
A risk of non-cash (fraud, declines, disputes, wrong room) and how it is lowered
Both need a receipt and a record

practical1.title: Open a cash point and take mixed payments with training money
practical1.brief: The Centre sets up a mock bar or front desk with a cash drawer, a POS or a calculator and a bill pad, and a training card terminal (or a mock one). Use training money only: J$ and US$ notes and coins clearly marked "TRAINING". The assessor gives the exchange rate for the day and any service charge to use; bills show GCT "at the current rate" as the assessor sets it. Each member in turn opens the cash point: counts and signs for a training float with the "supervisor" (another member), then takes four payments from "guests" (the other members, using scenario cards): a J$ cash bill, a J$ bill paid in US$ cash, a card payment, and a charge to a room account. Each member gives the correct change, issues a receipt and fills in a payments log. Photograph each stage below and add the photos and every member's float sheet and payments log to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Training money (J$ and US$ notes and coins marked "TRAINING") for a float of a set amount
A cash drawer or cash box, a POS or calculator, and bill pads or printed bills
A training or mock card terminal and made-up payment cards
Scenario cards for each payment, with made-up guest names and room numbers
Float sheets, payments logs, receipt books, bill folders and pens
The day's exchange rate and service charge, written by the assessor
photos: The float being counted and signed for with the "supervisor"
The drawer set out: notes face up and sorted by value, coins in sections
A cash payment, with the guest's note kept on top of the drawer
The working for a US$ payment, showing the rate given by the assessor
The card payment, with the "guest" keying in the PIN
A signed room charge bill, with the name and room number checked
Each member's completed payments log and receipts
checklist: Counted the float with the supervisor and signed the float sheet correctly
Set out the drawer neatly, with notes face up and sorted
Said the amount received aloud, checked the notes and kept the note on top until change was given
Worked out the US$ payment correctly at the assessor's rate and showed the working
Took the card payment without handling the PIN or writing down the card number
Checked the name and room number before the room charge and got the bill signed
Counted the change back correctly and gave a receipt for every payment
Was polite, kept guest details private and kept the drawer closed between sales
safety: Use only training money marked "TRAINING"; never bring real money into the task
Use made-up card numbers, guest names and room numbers only
Keep the drawer closed between sales and never leave it open and unattended
Keep the counter clear of cables and bags so nobody trips

practical2.title: Cash up, reconcile and hand over a drawer, and deal with problem payments
practical2.brief: Each member is given a drawer of training money (J$ and US$, marked "TRAINING") at the end of a mock shift, with a shift report, card slips, room charge slips and vouchers set up by the assessor. Some drawers have a planted shortage or overage. Each member, in turn, counts the drawer in a quiet corner, fills in a cash-up sheet, takes out the float, works out the takings, compares every total with the report, finds and records any difference, and prepares a sealed, signed takings bag with a deposit slip for the "safe". Then the group runs three short role plays, with members taking turns as cashier, guest and supervisor: a guest whose card is declined, a guest who hands over a note the assessor marks as "suspect", and a guest who says the bill is wrong. Photograph each stage below and add the photos and every member's cash-up sheet to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: A drawer or cash box of training money (J$ and US$ marked "TRAINING") for each member
A made-up shift report, card slips, room charge slips and vouchers for each drawer
Cash-up sheets, deposit slips, takings bags with seals, and pens
Role-play cards for a declined card, a suspect note and a disputed bill
Exchange rate for the day, written by the assessor
photos: A member counting the drawer in a quiet, secure place
The completed cash-up sheet, with J$ and US$ counted separately
The float counted out and set aside for the next shift
The totals compared with the shift report, and any difference written down
The sealed and signed takings bag with its deposit slip
Each role play: the declined card, the suspect note and the disputed bill
checklist: Counted the cash accurately by value and in each currency
Removed the correct float and worked out the takings correctly
Totalled card slips, room charges and vouchers and compared them with the report
Found any shortage or overage, recorded it honestly and reported it to the supervisor
Sealed, signed and recorded the takings bag correctly
Dealt with the declined card quietly and asked for another way to pay
Stayed calm with the suspect note, did not accuse the guest and called the supervisor
Listened to the guest with the disputed bill and checked each charge with them
safety: Use only training money; no real money, cards or guest details
Count cash away from the door and out of public view, as in a real property
In the role plays, nobody touches or grabs another person; stay calm and polite
Keep the work area tidy and the floor clear
